content.detail: A .pl source. The Prolog ENGINE is open and contract-level base predicates ship — they must, for conformance — but the genre bundles, the language corpora (CEFR/SRS data, the ~573 .pl seed files) and the generation heuristics do not. Every .pl in the tree is therefore classified by hand; a NEW one fails this gate until somebody writes down which side of the line it is on. The closed asset and the open asset have the same file extension, so the extension cannot decide.

dependency.reason: A BUNDLE INPUT, not a runtime import. corebridge/js/entry.js is the adapter esbuild reads when corebridge/tools/vendor-core-bundle.mjs re-vendors the core bundle; the specifier is resolved then, against a sibling @insimul/core checkout the vendoring tool is pointed at, and the artifact that ships (corebridge/vendor/core/insimul-core-bundle.js) carries ZERO bare specifiers — it is a closed graph, which this same scan verifies by reading it like any other file. @insimul/core is an OPEN repo (OPEN_SOURCE_STRATEGY.md names it the first to open), so the edge is open→open even at vendor time, and it is the dependency direction the README already describes: runtimes consume core.

dependency.detail: "@insimul/core" is not a Node builtin, and this repository declares no npm dependencies at all (there is no package.json), so it is not on the path a standalone clone can resolve
dependency.reason: As above — the contract-level radiant base templates, resolved at bundle time from the open core package. The allowance is per-SPECIFIER rather than per-file on purpose: a path-only allowance would silently bless every future bare import anybody adds to this file, which is the one place in the tree where adding one is easy.

dependency.detail: A build step that reaches the network. libinsimul is layer zero — four engine runtimes, the Rust server and every save file sit on it — so what it compiles must be what is committed (see CLAUDE.md, 'The engine source is VENDORED here'). A fetched input is a dependency the import graph cannot see, cannot pin and cannot audit, and it is how a repository that reads as self-contained stops being so. Every hit is classified by hand: the DEFAULT build (CMakeLists.txt, cmake/**) must have none at all.
dependency.reason: The ONE fetch in the tree that builds anything, and it is opt-in: this script clones upstream SWI-Prolog at its pin and installs it to a prefix, for the `-DINSIMUL_ENGINE=swipl` spike only. It is never invoked by `cmake --build`, the default engine is the VENDORED Trealla, and D20 (docs/SWIPL_MEASUREMENT.md) answered the spike NO — chief/252 stays parked. SWI is located, not vendored (CLAUDE.md, 'Two engines, one tree'), so nothing it downloads is committed here or shipped; cmake/swipl.cmake refuses a prefix that does not carry the pin file this script writes. Named rather than hidden because the shape is a real risk: a spike helper is exactly how a fetch becomes load-bearing later.

dependency.detail: "${CLOSED_BACKEND}" is not a Node builtin, and this repository declares no npm dependencies at all (there is no package.json), so it is not on the path a standalone clone can resolve
dependency.reason: THE FINDING THAT PROVES THE FIXTURE IS SAFE. The gate's own self-test has no basename exemption (see check-open-boundary.mjs's divergence 4), so it is audited like every other file — and what the scanner reads at these lines is the literal text `${CLOSED_BACKEND}`, a template placeholder, because the forbidden specifier is assembled by concatenation at run time and appears nowhere in the file's bytes. That is why the finding is `undeclared-dependency` and not `closed-repo-import`: had the fixture contained the real string, this entry would be the wrong rule and the gate would say so. A placeholder resolves to nothing and imports nothing; the file is a test that never runs its own fixtures as code.
